# Myosin motors fragment and compact membrane-bound actin filaments

## Authors

- Sven K Vogel<sup>1</sup> †
- Zdenek Petrasek<sup>1</sup>
- Fabian Heinemann<sup>1</sup>
- Petra Schwille<sup>1</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry Department of Cellular and Molecular Biophysics Martinsried Germany

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

10.7554/eLife.00116.001 Cell cortex remodeling during cell division is a result of myofilament-driven contractility of the cortical membrane-bound actin meshwork. Little is known about the interaction between individual myofilaments and membrane-bound actin filaments. Here we reconstituted a minimal actin cortex to directly visualize the action of individual myofilaments on membrane-bound actin filaments using TIRF microscopy. We show that synthetic myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin while processively moving along actin filaments. We propose a mechanism by which tension builds up between the ends of myofilaments, resulting in compressive stress exerted to single actin filaments, causing their buckling and breakage. Modeling of this mechanism revealed that sufficient force (∼20 pN) can be generated by single myofilaments to buckle and break actin filaments. This mechanism of filament fragmentation and compaction may contribute to actin turnover and cortex reorganization during cytokinesis. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.7554/eLife.00116.001

## Results

To mimic the cell cortex, we developed a ‘minimal actin cortex’ (MAC) consisting of actin filaments coupled to a supported lipid bilayer via biotin neutravidin bonds (Figure 1A). We used Alexa-488-phalloidin stabilized as well as non-stabilized (data not shown) actin filaments for the MAC composition. By varying the amount of biotinylated lipids present in the lipid bilayer, we have control over the density of the actin layer (Figure 1B). In order to understand the origin of contractility observed in cell cortices, we tested the response of the MAC upon addition of myosin motors. Rabbit muscle myosin II was purified and reassembled forming bipolar synthetic myofilaments with a typical length of 500–600 nm (Figure 1C). Time lapse imaging of MACs with various actin densities using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) showed a dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments, and subsequently the formation of actomyosin foci in an ATP-dependent manner immediately after addition of myofilaments (Figure 1D, Movie 1). Actin pattern formation occurred at ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM in systems where ATP is enzymatically regenerated (Table 1) in 94% of the experiments (n = 45 experiments). At higher and lower ATP concentrations, actin pattern formation in the MAC is absent. Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been also reported for experiments using actin and myofilaments in solution (Smith et al., 2007). Furthermore, an increase in fluorescence intensity along the remaining actin filament is often observed after a fragmentation event (Figure 2C, white arrowheads, Figure 2D,E). The fluorescence intensity proximal to the breakage site is approximately twice as high compared to the rest of the actin filament, suggesting that the fragment is dragged along the remaining actin filament by the myofilaments leading to its compaction (Figure 2C–E, Movie 3). We propose that fragmentation and compaction contribute to the observed coalescence of actin fragments into single foci during the dynamic rearrangement of the actin filaments (Figures 1D and 2A, Movies 1 and 2).

To determine how myofilaments execute fragmentation and compaction and to test whether these processes demand (concerted) actions of a multitude of myofilaments, we reduced the myofilament concentration to the single molecule level. Alexa-647 labeled myofilaments were added to MACs with low actin density and imaged by two-color TIRFM. Upon binding of single myofilaments to individual actin filaments, we observed directed movement of myofilaments along actin filaments and actin fragmentation at low ATP concentrations (

In contrast, at high ATP concentrations, processive movement of myofilaments was barely visible, and fragmentation of actin filaments was absent (supplementary text in ‘Material and methods’, Figure 5, Movie 5).

Shortly after binding of myofilaments, actin filaments deformed and eventually broke, indicating that the force generated by a single myofilament is sufficient to break an actin filament (Figure 3A, yellow arrowheads, Movie 4). Subsequently, the fluorescence signal of actin filaments proximal to the breakage site increased (Figure 3A, white arrowheads, Figure 3C). The detected increase in the fluorescence intensity of actin filaments implies that actin fragments are further dragged along the remaining actin filaments by the myofilaments during their movement (Figure 3A,D, Movie 4). We analyzed our TIRFM data in greater detail by tracking single myofilaments during their directed movement along an actin filament (Figure 3B, (Rogers et al., 2007)) and determining the velocity from the trajectories (Figure 3C, red curve). Simultaneously, the fluorescence intensity in the green (actin) channel of the area occupied by the myofilament during its movement was measured, indicating breakage events as the dragged fragment leads to an increase of fluorescence proximal to the breakage site (Figure 3C, blue and black curve). The velocity fluctuates during the movement of the myofilament along the actin filament (Figure 3C, red curve), whereby acceleration events (Figure 3C, red arrowheads) are closely followed by an increase in the actin fluorescence, indicating that a breakage event occurred (Figure 3C, black arrows, blue and black curve). We hypothesize that phases of increasing tension between the ends of the myofilament lead to deformation of the actin filament and coincide with a decrease in velocity, while the phases of tension release immediately after actin filament breakage may result in acceleration of the myofilament (Figure 3C,D).

In order to explain the buckling and eventual breakage of the actin filament, we propose the following model: The myosin filament aligns parallel to the actin filament and interacts with it via the myosin heads ((Sellers and Kachar, 1990), Figure 3D). One end of the myofilament, which we will refer to as the ‘leading end’, is oriented towards the actin plus end (barbed end), as the filaments in a muscle, and can therefore walk along the actin filament while hydrolyzing ATP (Figure 3D). The other end of the myofilament, which we will refer to as the ‘trailing end’, separated from the leading end by the approximately 160 nm long bare zone (Al-Khayat et al., 2010) without myosin heads, is oriented in the opposite direction. While the trailing end still interacts with the actin filament, its opposite orientation results in a much slower directed motion towards the actin plus end (Spudich et al., 1985; Sellers and Kachar, 1990). Every myosin head independently follows the biochemical cycle consisting of ATP hydrolysis, binding to actin, powerstroke accompanied by phosphate dissociation, ADP dissociation, ATP binding, and finally detachment from actin ((Howard, 2001), Figure 8). We assume that the heads on the trailing end still interact with the actin filament and go through the same cycle, but either do not perform steps that would lead to a processive motion (probability of making a step pst=0), or make steps with a small probability (pst=0.1). When a myosin head makes a step (step size d = 5 nm (Howard, 2001)) it tries to move the whole myosin filament towards the actin plus end, but other attached myosin heads are holding it back, thus generating friction (Figure 3D). The myofilament trailing end functions mainly as a source of friction (an effective ‘brake’), but is also moved towards the plus end by the pulling force exerted by the leading end (Figure 3D). Since mainly the leading end is actively moving and the trailing end is either passively pulled (pst=0) or contributes only weakly to its own motion (pst=0.1), tension builds up within the myofilament, and is transferred onto the actin filament as a compressive force. If sufficiently high, this compressive force can cause buckling, and finally breakage, of the actin filament (Figure 3D). After the breakage, the leading end can move unhindered further towards the plus end, while dragging along the broken-off part of the actin filament attached to the trailing end (Figure 3D). The trailing end can also attach again to the actin and further breakage events on the same filament can follow.

## Discussion

In our in vitro study we provide a potential mechanism how actin turnover in cells may be mediated by myofilament driven actin fragmentation. To bend and break the actin filament, the myofilament has to be attached to the actin for sufficient time, and sufficient force has to be generated, requiring a certain mean number of heads being attached to actin at any given time. Given the small number of interacting myosin heads this translates to a requirement that a large fraction of heads is in the bound state. In our assay this was achieved with low ATP concentrations. It is tempting to speculate that actin breakage by myofilaments in vivo is governed by the ATP level in the cell. Recent evidence exists that ATP levels indeed vary significantly inside living cells (Imamura et al., 2009). However, physiological ATP concentrations, derived from methods that provide averaged ATP levels with no high spatial and temporal resolution from cell extracts, are usually found in the millimolar range (Beis and Newsholme, 1975). Here it is important to mention that skeletal muscle myosin II (used in this study) has a lower duty ratio and is therefore less processive than non-muscle myosin in cells (Harris and Warshaw, 1993; Wang et al., 2003). By lowering the ATP concentration in our assay, we increased the duty ratio of our myofilaments and thereby made them more processive (supplementary text in ‘Material and methods’, Figure 5, Movie 5), similar to non-muscle myosin, which is in line with previous studies (Humphrey et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2007; Soares e Silva et al., 2011). Moreover, processivity of myofilaments in animal cells may be also controlled by phosphorylation of myosin light chains through other proteins that modify the kinetic rates of the biochemical cycle and thereby increase the duty ratio of the myosins shifting the observed behavior to a region of high physiological ATP concentrations (Tan et al., 1992; DeBiasio et al., 1996; Matsumura et al., 2001).

Our simulations show that the model of interaction between the actin and myosin filaments described in the text is plausible given the quantitative parameter values known from literature (rate constants). Most importantly, it shows that sufficient force needed to bend and break the actin filament can be generated by a single myofilament, assuming only the difference in the interaction between the leading and trailing myofilament ends (making a step vs not making a step). This result implies that neither actin nor myosin attachment to a support or any other rigid structure is necessary for the observed process. The forces act within a single myofilament. Binding of the actin filaments to the membrane provides confinement of the filaments to a plane, without rigidly tethering the filaments to a support or a scaffold. The motion of actin is only restricted by the effectively higher viscosity of the membrane compared to the buffer solution. The simulation further yields quantitative details of the model, for example, the mean fractions of myosin heads in the six possible states (

In conclusion, our findings show the distinct functions that myosin motors can execute. In our minimal system, myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin. We directly show that single myofilaments can interact with actin in such a way that sufficient force can be generated to break the filament, without either the myofilament or the actin being firmly attached to a solid support or scaffold. We suggest that fragmentation and compaction by myofilaments contributes to the observed large-scale pattern formation of actomyosin networks also in other in vitro systems (Backouche et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2007; Soares e Silva et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2012). In vivo breakage of actin bundles has been shown to occur in neuronal growth cones in a myosin II dependent manner, and is thought to be important for recycling actin (Medeiros et al., 2006). We propose that the observed fragmentation and compaction of membrane-bound actin filaments by myosins in our in vitro system may serve as a possible general mechanism for actin turnover and actin cell cortex remodeling.

## Material and methods

## Details of the experiments

Traditionally, single muscle myosin II motors are described as non-processive motors (Howard, 2001). By assembling myosin motors into filaments, the myofilaments become processive due to the coupling of a higher number of myosin heads that are in contact with the actin filament. In our minimal system directed movement accompanied by actin filament fragmentation only occurred at low ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM (Figure 3, Table 1, Movie 3). The lower ATP concentrations are expected to increase the duration of the actin-bound post-working stroke state of the myosin head, thus increasing the duty ratio and processivity (Howard, 2001). Extremely low ATP concentrations are on the other hand not sufficient for myosin motor activity. To check the effect of ATP concentration on processivity we added Alexa-647 labeled myofilaments to medium density MACs and tracked (Rogers et al., 2007) the movement of individual myofilaments at low (1 µM) and high (4 mM) ATP concentrations (Figure 5, Movie 5). (Note that fragmentation and compaction of actin filaments only occurred at low ATP concentrations). Comparison of the trajectories illustrates that low ATP trajectories are on average longer than high ATP trajectories indicating a higher processivity at low ATP conditions (Figure 5, Movie 5). Moreover the number of tracked myofilaments at low ATP concentration with a dwell time greater than 900 ms was more than six times higher than at high ATP concentration suggesting a higher duty ratio at low ATP levels (n = 681 at low ATP, n = 102 at high ATP; Figure 5, Movie 5). High ATP concentrations therefore lead to a faster detachment of myofilaments from actin filaments than at low ATP concentrations (Movie 5). We propose that the increase in processivity due to ATP deprivation is necessary for the processive movement and a prerequisite for fragmentation and compaction of actin filaments.

## Details of the model

## Biochemical cycle

In the model of the myofilament interaction with actin, we assume that each active myosin head goes through the following biochemical cycle consisting of six head states (Howard, 2001). The six states are schematized in Figure 8. Unbound myosin head with ATP (state 1) hydrolyses ATP with the rate k1 = 100 s−1 (state 2), binds to the actin filament with the rate k2 = 30 s−1 (state 3), rapidly releases phosphate while performing a powerstroke with rate k3 = 104 s−1 (state 4), releases ADP with the rate k4 = 1000 s−1 (state 5), binds ATP with the rate k5 = kt [ATP], where kt = 4 μM−1 s−1, (state 6), and dissociates from the actin filament with the rate k6 = 2000 s−1 (state 1). These rates determine the average time the myosin heads spend in every state (Figure 9). In this simple model the rates are assumed to be independent of the strain of the myosin head. The myosin step size is d = 5 nm (Howard, 2001). The myosin heads of the leading myofilament end always perform a step as a result of the powerstroke between the states 3 and 4. The heads of the trailing end either do not make a step (the probability of making a step pst=0), or, in separate simulations, make a step with the probability pst=0.1. This value is based on the observations that the trailing myofilament end moves along actin with approximately ten-times slower speed than the leading end (Sellers and Kachar, 1990).

## Mechanical equillibrium

Every myosin head attached to the actin filament is described as a spring with a spring constant equal to the myosin head stiffness κ = 1 pN nm−1 (Kaya and Higuchi, 2010). After every step and after every detachment of a myosin head the forces are equilibrated by moving the myofilament along the actin filament. The result is a net movement of the whole myofilament towards the actin plus end, with flucuating tension force, velocity and number of attached myosin heads, the mean values of which depend on the ATP concentration.

## Number of myosin heads on the myofilament

The median length of the myofilaments determined with AFM was 560 nm (Figure 1C). Assuming the length of the bare zone without myosin heads in the central part of the myofilament to be 160 nm (Al-Khayat et al., 2010), both ends of the myofilament are 200 nm long. With four myosin head pairs around the myofilament circumference per every 14.5 nm (Woodhead et al., 2005), there are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament. Assuming further that only those heads oriented towards one side, that is, one quarter, can interact with the actin filament, and that only one head of the head pair is favorably oriented to interact, we estimate the average number of interacting heads as 30 per myofilament.

## Buckling force

In order to estimate the force needed to bend the actin filament, we model it as a flexible rod with bending rigidity EI = 60 nN μm2, determined from the persistence length of actin: lp = EI/(kT) = 15 μm (Yanagida et al., 1984). The force needed to buckle and break the filament is F = π2 EI/l2. With the length l of the myofilament bare zone of 160 nm, this gives a force of 23 pN. Actin filaments break when the radius of curvature of a bent filament decreases below 0.18 μm (Arai et al., 1999) corresponding to the curvature 1/r = 5.6 μm−1.

## Results of the simulations

In order to find out if the tension within the myofilament transferred onto the actin filament as a compressive force can become sufficiently high to bend and break the actin filament, we performed two types of simulations.

In the first case, bending of the filament was not allowed and no limit was imposed on the compression force within the actin filament. This allowed us to determine the forces that can be reached by this model. In the second case, the actin filament was allowed to bend when the force of 23 pN was exceeded. Actin bending was modeled by decreasing the distance between the leading and trailing ends of the myofilament, thus relaxing the stress and reducing the force down to 23 pN.

In case when bending was not allowed, the average force increased with decreasing ATP concentration, and also with the increasing number of myosin heads (Figure 4A). For 30 myosin heads, the force of 23 pN, neccessary to bend the filament, could be reached at ATP concentrations of approximately 3 µM or lower (Figure 4A).

In the ATP concentration range used in the experiments here (<100 µM, see also Table 1) the average velocity of myofilament increased approximately linearly with ATP concentration, independently of the number of myosin heads, or of the fact whether actin bending was allowed or not (Figure 6A). The average fraction of myosin heads attached to actin increased with decreasing ATP concentration (Figure 6B), and since the myosin heads act independently of each other and of the forces involved, was also independent of number of myosin heads and actin bending.

When the actin filament was allowed to bend, the maximum force was not permitted to exceed 23 pN (Figure 4B). At low ATP concentration, the generated force was sufficiently high to continuously bend the actin filament, steadily increasing the curvature above the breakage threshold (Figure 7A). At intermediate ATP concentrations, the force fluctuating near the threshold caused fluctuations in curvature, at times exceeding the curvature threshold and then relaxing again to a straight filament configuration (Figures 4C and 7B). At even higher ATP concentrations, the threshold force was reached for too short periods for sufficiently high curvature to develop (Figures 4D and 7C).

The results for the scenario where the myosin heads of the trailing end can make a step towards the plus actin end with the probability pst=0.1 are very similar to those with pst=0. The differences are that the generated forces are slightly lower (Figure 4A,B) and the mean velocity slightly higher (Figure 6A).

## Actin preparation and labeling

Rabbit skeletal muscle actin monomers (Molecular Probes) and biotinylated rabbit actin monomers (tebu-bio [Cytoskeleton Inc.]) were mixed in a 5:1 (actin:biotin-actin) ratio. Polymerization of the mixture (39.6 µM) was induced in F-Buffer containing 50 mM KCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 1 mM ATP, 10 mM Tris–HCl buffer (pH 7.5). The biotinylated actin filaments were labeled with Alexa-Fluor 488 Phalloidin (Molecular Probes) according to the manufacturer protocol. Finally, 2 µM (refers to monomers) of Alexa-488-Phalloidin labeled biotinylated actin filaments were obtained.

## Myosin preparation and labeling

Myosin was purified from rabbit skeletal muscle tissue as previously described (Smith et al., 2007). Myosin activity was tested by a classical motility assay where myosins bound to a nitrocellulose coated glass surface of a perfusion chamber (tebu-bio [Cytoskeleton Inc.]) propel actin filaments. Movement of actin filaments indicated integrity of the myosin motors (data not shown). Myofilament assembly was induced in reaction buffer containing 50 mM KCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 10 mM Tris–HCl buffer (pH 7.5), and depending on the experiments various amounts of regenerated ATP and an oxygen scavenger system. Equilibration of the mixture for approximately 30 min gave us a median length of 560 nm in our system (Figure 1C).

Myosins were labeled with thiol-reactive dyes AlexaFluor 488 C5-maleimide as well as AlexaFluor 647 C2-maleimide (both Molecular Probes). The labeling reactions were performed in a slight variation according to the manufacturer protocol. In brief, the thiol-reactive dyes were dissolved in DMSO to 10 mM concentration and stored at −80°C. The myosin stock (14.99 µM in 50% glycerol) was diluted to 2 µM in reaction buffer containing 50 mM KCl, 10 mM Tris–HCl buffer (pH 7.5) and 2 mM MgCl2. The solution was deoxygated for 15 min under vacuum and put into N2 environment. 15 times molar excess (30 µM) of TCEP (tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine, Molecular Probes) was added to the solution and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. 25-fold molar excess to reach 50 µM of the maleimide dyes were added dropwise to the solution while it was stirred and incubated overnight at 4°C. Labeled myofilaments were separated from the remaining dyes by gel filtration to obtain 1 µM (refers to single myosins) labeled myofilaments. Activity of labeled myosins was confirmed by motility and actin pattern formation assays. Aliquots were frozen and stored at −80 °C.

## MAC (Minimal actin cortex) preparation

For MAC preparation a chamber consisting of a cut 1.5 ml Eppendorf tube glued to an air plasma cleaned glass cover slip (22 × 22 mm, #1.5, Menzel Gläser, Thermo Fisher, Braunschweig, Germany) was built. For planar, glass supported lipid bilayer formation molar ratios of the lipids (purchased from Avanti Polar Lipids, Alabaster, AL) Egg PC (99.99, 99.9 and 99 mol%) and DSPE-PEG(2000)-Biotin (0.01, 0.1 and 1 mol%) were dissolved in chloroform (total 10 mg/ml of lipids), dried under nitrogen flux for 30 min and subsequently put into vacuum for 30 min. Lipids were then rehydrated in reaction buffer containing 50 mM KCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 10 mM Tris–HCl buffer (pH 7.5) and resuspended by vigorous vortexing. To obtain SUVs (small unilamellar vesicles) the suspension was exposed to sonication in a water bath at room temperature. 10 µl of the suspension were mixed with 90 µl reaction buffer and placed onto the glass cover slip of the chamber. CaCl2 to a final concentration of 0.1 mM was added to induce fusion of the SUVs and the formation of a lipid bilayer on the glass surface. The sample was washed several times with a total volume of approximately 2 ml reaction buffer in order to remove unfused vesicles. After washing, 2 µg of Neutravidin (Molecular Probes) dissolved in 200 µl reaction buffer was added to the sample and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. The sample was washed several times with >2 ml reaction buffer to remove unbound Neutravidin. Then 10–50 µl of 2 µM (refers to monomers) Alexa-488-phalloidin labeled biotinylated actin filaments were added to the lipid bilayer and incubated for 1 h. The sample was carefully washed with approximately 1–2 ml reaction buffer to remove unbound actin filaments.

## Actin fragmentation and pattern formation assay

Alexa-647 (and Alexa-488) labeled myofilaments and/or non-labeled myofilaments of various concentrations (as indicated) dissolved in 200 µl reaction buffer were added to the MAC and imaged by TIRF microscopy. The reaction buffer contained 0.1–1 µM ATP (see also Table 1), an ATP regenerating system consisting of 20 mM Creatine phosphate (Sigma) and 0.1 mg ml−1 Creatine phospho kinase (Sigma) to keep the ATP concentration constant and an oxygen scavenger system (glucose oxidase (165 U ml−1) catalase (2,170 U ml−1), β-D-glucose (0.4% wt/vol) and Trolox (2 mM), all from Sigma) to reduce photobleaching of the Alexa dyes. Actin rearrangements and fragmentation occurred immediately after addition of the myofilaments.

## TIRF microscopy

Two color TIRF microscopy was carried out on a custom-made setup built around an Axiovert 200 microscope (Zeiss), for details see (Loose et al., 2011). A α Plan-Apochromat 100×/NA 1.46 oil immersion objective and 488 nm and 647 nm laser lines were used for excitation of the labeled probes. The exposure times were either 50 ms or 100 ms, and the time intervals between each recorded frame ranged from 200–400 ms for different experiments.

## AFM imaging

Atomic force microscopy was performed using a NanoWizard AFM system (JPK Instruments, Berlin, Germany). The AFM head was mounted on top of a stable cast-iron microscope stage and combined with a LSM 510 confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany). Soft, rectangular silicon cantilevers (CSC38/noAl, Micromash, Tallin, Estonia) with a nominal spring constant of 0.03 N/m were used. The cantilever sensitivity in V/m was determined before each measurement. The spring constant was calibrated by using the thermal fluctuations method. Clean, circular glass cover slips (d = 24 mm, #1.5, Menzel Gläser, Thermo Fisher, Braunschweig, Germany) were hydrophilized by air plasma cleaning. The AFM fluid cell was assembled by using the glass slide and filled with 400 µl of the reaction buffer. Directly before AFM imaging, myofilaments were diluted with reaction buffer to a concentration of 10 nM. 5 µL of 10 nM myofilaments in reaction buffer were added to the fluid cell. In experiments with combined AFM and fluorescence imaging, Alexa-488 labeled myofilaments were used. After 15 min incubation most of the myofilaments adhered to the hydrophilic surface, residual non-adherent filaments were removed by washing with reaction buffer. AFM imaging was performed in contact mode with a scan rate of 1 Hz. The imaging forces were kept very low (<0.5 nN) by continuously adjusting the deflection setpoint and using optimized feedback gains. Raw AFM images were line and plane fitted by using the open source software Gwyddion (www.gwyddion.net).

## Myofilament length determination

Length histograms of myofilaments were obtained from confocal images of Alexa-488 labeled myofilaments prepared as described in the AFM imaging section. Confocal microscopy was performed using a LSM 510 Meta system (Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany) with a 40× water immersion objective (C-Apochromat, 40×/1.2, Carl Zeiss). The 488 nm line of an Argon-ion laser was used to excite the sample. Fluorescence excitation and emission were separated using a microscope build-in dichroic mirror (HFT 488/633) and band pass filter (BP 505–550) in front of the detector. Myofilament length measurement of the AFM images was manually performed with the software Gwyddion. Myofilament length distribution of the confocal images with xy-pixel size of 110 nm was obtained manually using Image J. The accuracy of the length determination based on confocal microscopy was verified by colocalization with AFM images. Identical lengths of the filaments were obtained using both methods (Pearson's r = 0.99, n = 47) and therefore justified bulk measurements using confocal microscopy.

## Data analysis

Data analysis was performed with Image J (Rasband, W.S., National Institutes of Health, USA, http://imagej.nih.gov/ij) and custom written scripts in Igor Pro 6.0 (WaveMetrics, Lake Oswego, USA) and MatLab. Actin filament length measurement (Figure 2B) was performed using the NeuronJ Image J plugin, for details see (Meijering et al., 2004). The fluorescence intensity profiles for Figure 2D,E (main text) were obtained using the segmented line tool and plot profile command in Image J. To determine the fluorescence intensity in the area occupied by a myofilament (Figure 3C [main text]) a custom written macro in Image J was used. In brief, the image sequence in the 647 nm channel of the Alexa-647 labeled myofilament (red) was converted to 8-bit, binarized by using a threshold filter and an area selection (corresponding to the myofilament) for each binary image was created. The mean fluorescence intensity in the corresponding 488 nm channel images of the Alexa-488-phalloidin labeled actin filaments (green) was computed in the selected area. Smoothing of intensity profiles in Figure 3C was conducted using a sliding-average smoothing algorithm (interval 2 s) implemented in Igor Pro.

Myofilaments for the velocity analysis were tracked using a custom written program by Rogers et al. (for details see (Rogers et al., 2007)). The radial velocity vt was computed from the myofilament trajectories xt, yt, where t is the discrete sampling time with an interval Δt = 0.2 s. The radial change in position was computed by Δrt = ((xt+nΔt − xt)2 + (yt+nΔt − yt)2)1/2. The radial velocity was obtained from vt = Δrt/nΔt. Computation intervals nΔt with n = 20 were chosen to reduce the noise induced by small fluctuations in the positions.

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for choosing to send your work entitled “Myosin Motors Fragment and Compact Membrane-Bound Actin Filaments” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been evaluated by a Senior Editor and 3 reviewers, one of whom is a member of eLife's Board of Reviewing Editors.

The Reviewing Editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing Editor has assembled the following comments based on the reviewers' reports.

The referees agree that your work provides an interesting mechanism for compaction of actin filaments by myofilaments and how this might apply to actin organization at the cell cortex. We list the concerns below:

1. There is concern at the lack of quantification of the major experiment. There is a need to quantify these results. How many times were these experiments performed and how many times were the effects of myofilaments on actin filaments observed?

2. It is not clear how much the simulations have helped the paper. It would be more useful if the simulations lead to some testable hypothesis that then expand/strengthen/fine-tune the model. This needs to be clarified.

Below are a number of important points pertaining to the experiments, all of which seem to be on point and require resolution.

3. Most experiments (at least those employed to derive mechanism) were performed in near rigor conditions. Given that the km for myosin-II nucleotide-binding is in the tens of micro-molar, the use of ∼3 micro-molar ATP is a concern. With respect to muscle (the source of the myosin-II in these experiments), the ATP concentration is ∼5 mM and >100 micro-molar in non-muscle cells.

The authors predict that 30 molecules of myosin-II (per mini-filament) are in contact with an actin filament. However, the force estimate (23 pN) for buckling only reflects that of 5–6 active heads. In other words, >80% of the myosin heads are in rigor.

This type of tension/buckling is what is expected (and previously seen) in traditional motility assays when ATP is kept low. This point assumes the authors are using fully active myosin-II preparations (based on their testing of preparations).

4. The authors use myosin-II mini-filaments that are free in solution, which forces them to use rigor conditions. Given what the authors are aiming to reproduce, shouldn't myosin-II be tethered independently of actin in their assays (as it is presumably to some degree at the cell division site, given that myosin localization is often tail-dependent and actin-independent)? This approach would invoke tension (with actin and myosin tethered) reflecting the force-velocity relationship of myosin-II, an effect that is more likely seen in cells.

5. How closely does the actin and myosin concentration used reflect the in vivo actomyosin density at the cell cortex?

The choice of muscle myosin-II seems specialized; perhaps non-muscle myosin-II would be best for reconstituting general cellular behavior?

6. We generally felt that the conditions used in the experiments were not very physiological and hard to reconcile with what is probably found in cells. Two types are experiments need to be performed to further validate the conclusions: (a) perform the study with non-muscle myosin II at physiological ATP concentrations and (b) attempt to link myosin II, rather than F-actin, to the minimal cortex to observe effects on F-actin shortening, buckling, and turnover.

claims.claim: The myosin heads of the leading myofilament end always perform a step as a result of the powerstroke between the states 3 and 4.
claims.source: The myosin heads of the leading myofilament end always perform a step as a result of the powerstroke between the states 3 and 4.
claims.evidence: This is an assumption in the model based on known myosin motor function.

claims.claim: The heads of the trailing end either do not make a step (probability pst=0), or make a step with the probability pst=0.1.
claims.source: The heads of the trailing end either do not make a step (the probability of making a step pst=0), or, in separate simulations, make a step with the probability pst=0.1.
claims.evidence: This is an assumption in the model based on observations from cited literature.

claims.claim: The trailing myofilament end moves along actin with approximately ten-times slower speed than the leading end.
claims.source: This value is based on the observations that the trailing myofilament end moves along actin with approximately ten-times slower speed than the leading end (Sellers and Kachar, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from cited literature.

claims.claim: Every myosin head attached to the actin filament is described as a spring with a spring constant equal to the myosin head stiffness κ = 1 pN nm−1.
claims.source: Every myosin head attached to the actin filament is described as a spring with a spring constant equal to the myosin head stiffness κ = 1 pN nm−1 (Kaya and Higuchi, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a parameter from cited literature used in the model.

claims.claim: The median length of the myofilaments determined with AFM was 560 nm.
claims.source: The median length of the myofilaments determined with AFM was 560 nm (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The length of the bare zone without myosin heads in the central part of the myofilament is 160 nm.
claims.source: Assuming the length of the bare zone without myosin heads in the central part of the myofilament to be 160 nm (Al-Khayat et al., 2010), both ends of the myofilament are 200 nm long.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural information from cited literature.

claims.claim: There are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament.
claims.source: With four myosin head pairs around the myofilament circumference per every 14.5 nm (Woodhead et al., 2005), there are on average 110 head pairs on each myofilament.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from structural information from cited literature.

claims.claim: The average number of interacting heads is 30 per myofilament.
claims.source: Assuming further that only those heads oriented towards one side, that is, one quarter, can interact with the actin filament, and that only one head of the head pair is favorably oriented to interact, we estimate the average number of interacting heads as 30 per myofilament.
claims.evidence: This is estimated from structural considerations and calculations.

claims.claim: Actin filaments have a persistence length of 15 μm.
claims.source: In order to estimate the force needed to bend the actin filament, we model it as a flexible rod with bending rigidity EI = 60 nN μm2, determined from the persistence length of actin: lp = EI/(kT) = 15 μm (Yanagida et al., 1984).
claims.evidence: This is a known physical property from cited literature.

claims.claim: Actin filaments break when the radius of curvature of a bent filament decreases below 0.18 μm.
claims.source: Actin filaments break when the radius of curvature of a bent filament decreases below 0.18 μm (Arai et al., 1999) corresponding to the curvature 1/r = 5.6 μm−1.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data from cited literature.

claims.claim: The average force increased with decreasing ATP concentration and with the increasing number of myosin heads when bending was not allowed in simulations.
claims.source: In case when bending was not allowed, the average force increased with decreasing ATP concentration, and also with the increasing number of myosin heads (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The average velocity of myofilament increased approximately linearly with ATP concentration in the ATP concentration range used in the experiments (<100 µM).
claims.source: In the ATP concentration range used in the experiments here (<100 µM, see also Table 1) the average velocity of myofilament increased approximately linearly with ATP concentration, independently of the number of myosin heads, or of the fact whether actin bending was allowed or not (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The average fraction of myosin heads attached to actin increased with decreasing ATP concentration.
claims.source: The average fraction of myosin heads attached to actin increased with decreasing ATP concentration (Figure 6B), and since the myosin heads act independently of each other and of the forces involved, was also independent of number of myosin heads and actin bending.
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Actin pattern formation occurred in 94% of the experiments (n = 45 experiments).
claims.source: Actin pattern formation occurred at ATP concentrations between 0.1–1 µM in systems where ATP is enzymatically regenerated (Table 1) in 94% of the experiments (n = 45 experiments).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical summary of experimental results.

claims.claim: Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been reported for experiments using actin and myofilaments in solution.
claims.source: Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been also reported for experiments using actin and myofilaments in solution (Smith et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claims.claim: Biotinylated actin filaments are coupled to a supported lipid bilayer containing biotinylated lipids via Neutravidin in the MAC.
claims.source: Biotinylated actin filaments are coupled to a supported lipid bilayer (Egg PC) containing biotinylated lipids (DSPE-PEG(2000)-Biotin) via Neutravidin.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The increase of actin filament densities corresponds to an increase in the amount of DSPE-PEG200-Biotin in the membrane.
claims.source: The increase of actin filament densities (left to right) corresponds to an increase in the amount of DSPE-PEG200-Biotin (low = 0.01 mol%, medium = 0.1 mol%, high = 1 mol%) in the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Alexa-488-phalloidin stabilized actin filaments were used for the MAC composition.
claims.source: We used Alexa-488-phalloidin stabilized as well as non-stabilized (data not shown) actin filaments for the MAC composition.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental materials used.

results.result: The authors developed a minimal actin cortex (MAC) system consisting of biotinylated actin filaments coupled to a supported lipid bilayer via neutravidin bonds, with controllable actin density achieved by varying biotinylated lipid concentration. Synthetic myofilaments were assembled from rabbit muscle myosin II with typical lengths of 500-600 nm.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9 and C77-C79 describe the experimental system design with clear methodological details. The MAC system is well-characterized with appropriate controls for actin density (Figure 1B) and myofilament length measurements via AFM (Figure 1C). The experimental design is sound and reproducible.

results.result: Addition of myofilaments to MACs resulted in dynamic actin rearrangement and actomyosin foci formation in an ATP-dependent manner, occurring specifically at ATP concentrations between 0.1-1 µM (94% of experiments, n=45) but absent at higher or lower concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C75 are well-supported by systematic experimental observations across multiple conditions (Table 1, Figure 1D). The ATP concentration dependence is clearly demonstrated with adequate sample size (n=45) and high reproducibility (94%). The use of ATP regeneration systems ensures constant ATP levels during experiments.

results.result: In low-density MACs, myofilaments caused actin filament breakage and compaction, with fluorescence intensity approximately doubling at breakage sites, indicating that fragments are dragged along remaining filaments. This fragmentation and compaction contributes to coalescence of actin into foci.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are supported by direct experimental observations (Figure 2, Movies 2-3) across all experiments (n=21). The fluorescence intensity measurements provide quantitative evidence for fragment compaction. However, the mechanistic link to foci formation (C16) is somewhat inferential, though reasonably supported by the data.

results.result: Single-molecule experiments revealed that individual myofilaments exhibit processive directed movement along actin filaments and cause fragmentation specifically at low ATP concentrations (0.1-1 µM). At low ATP, myofilament trajectories were longer (n=681 with dwell time >900 ms) compared to high ATP (n=102), indicating increased processivity. At high ATP concentrations, processive movement was barely visible and fragmentation was absent.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 and C54-C58 are well-supported by single-molecule tracking data (Figures 3, 5, Movies 4-5). The quantitative comparison of trajectory lengths and dwell times provides strong evidence for ATP-dependent processivity. The correlation between velocity fluctuations and fluorescence intensity increases (C21) is demonstrated but the temporal resolution may limit precise determination of causality.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanism where the leading end of the myofilament walks processively toward the actin plus end while the trailing end (separated by a 160 nm bare zone) moves much slower, creating tension within the myofilament. This tension is transferred as compressive force to the actin filament, causing buckling and breakage. After breakage, the leading end drags the broken fragment along the remaining filament.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C30 present a mechanistic model supported by experimental observations (velocity-fluorescence correlations in C21-C22) and established structural knowledge (C23-C26 from literature). The model is internally consistent and explains the observed phenomena. However, direct visualization of the proposed tension buildup is not provided, making some aspects inferential.

results.result: Computational modeling using established physical parameters (actin bending rigidity EI=60 nN·µm², bare zone length 160 nm) calculated that 23 pN force is needed to buckle actin filaments. Simulations showed this force can be reached at ATP concentrations ≤3 µM with 30 myosin heads, with force increasing as ATP concentration decreases and myosin head number increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 and C72 are supported by computational simulations using well-established physical parameters from literature (C31, C70, C71). The force calculation (C32) follows standard buckling theory (Euler buckling formula). The simulations systematically explore parameter space (Figure 4A, 7A-C) and results are consistent with experimental observations of ATP-dependent fragmentation.

results.result: The computational model assumes myosin heads undergo a six-state biochemical cycle with 5 nm step size, with leading end heads always stepping and trailing end heads either not stepping (pst=0) or stepping with probability 0.1. Model parameters include 30 interacting heads per myofilament (calculated from 560 nm median length, 160 nm bare zone, and structural data) and myosin head stiffness κ=1 pN/nm.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C69 describe model parameters and assumptions based on established literature values and reasonable structural calculations. The six-state cycle (C60) is standard for myosin. The estimate of 30 interacting heads (C69) involves several assumptions about head orientation but is transparently derived from structural data. The differential stepping probability (C62-C63) is the key novel assumption, justified by literature on trailing end behavior (C64).

results.result: The modeling demonstrates that single myofilaments can generate sufficient force to break actin filaments without requiring attachment to rigid supports, with forces acting within the myofilament itself. The membrane provides planar confinement through increased viscosity rather than rigid tethering.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C43-C48 present key conclusions from the modeling work. The simulations successfully demonstrate force generation sufficient for breakage (C44) using literature-derived parameters (C43). The conclusion that rigid attachment is unnecessary (C45) is well-supported by the model mechanics. The interpretation of membrane role (C47-C48) is reasonable though the effective viscosity is not quantified.

results.result: Simulations showed that myofilament velocity increased approximately linearly with ATP concentration below 100 µM, independent of myosin head number or actin bending. The fraction of attached myosin heads increased with decreasing ATP concentration, also independent of head number and bending.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by simulation results (Figure 6A-B). The linear velocity-ATP relationship is consistent with standard myosin kinetics in the low ATP regime. The independence from head number and bending conditions strengthens the conclusions. These results align with experimental observations of ATP-dependent processivity.

results.result: Skeletal muscle myosin II has lower duty ratio than non-muscle myosin, but lowering ATP concentration increases duty ratio and processivity by increasing duration of the actin-bound post-working stroke state. This increased processivity is necessary for processive movement and is a prerequisite for fragmentation and compaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 and C55 are supported by established literature and experimental observations (Figure 5, Movie 5). The mechanistic explanation (C55) is well-established. Claim C59 proposes that increased processivity is necessary for fragmentation, which is supported by the correlation between low ATP (high processivity) and fragmentation occurrence, though direct causality is not definitively proven.

results.result: While physiological ATP concentrations are typically millimolar, ATP levels vary significantly in living cells. The authors speculate that in vivo, myofilament processivity may be controlled by phosphorylation of myosin light chains, which could shift the observed behavior to higher physiological ATP concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 cite literature on ATP levels but highlight a tension between the low ATP concentrations required in vitro (0.1-1 µM) and typical cellular ATP levels (millimolar). Claim C42 is explicitly speculative about phosphorylation control. While the speculation is reasonable and cited, no experimental evidence is provided to bridge this gap, leaving the physiological relevance uncertain.

results.result: Synthetic myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin while processively moving along filaments. The proposed mechanism involves tension buildup between myofilament ends resulting in compressive stress that causes actin buckling and breakage. Modeling revealed single myofilaments can generate sufficient force (~20 pN) for this process.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 summarize the main findings. C2 is directly supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript. C3 presents the proposed mechanism supported by both experimental correlations and modeling. C4 is supported by computational simulations using established parameters. Together these claims represent the core contribution of the work.

results.result: The authors propose that this mechanism of filament fragmentation and compaction may contribute to actin turnover and cortex reorganization during cytokinesis, and may explain pattern formation in other in vitro actomyosin systems. They suggest it could serve as a general mechanism for actin turnover and cortex remodeling, noting that myosin II-dependent actin bundle breakage occurs in neuronal growth cones.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C49, and C51 are explicitly speculative about biological relevance and generalizability. While C50 cites in vivo evidence of myosin II-dependent breakage, no direct experiments connect the in vitro mechanism to cellular processes. The speculation is reasonable and well-motivated, but lacks experimental validation in cellular contexts or with non-muscle myosin II.

results.result: Cell cortex remodeling during cell division results from myofilament-driven contractility of the cortical membrane-bound actin meshwork. The actin cortex consists of a thin actin meshwork bound to the inner cytosolic face of the plasma membrane by various anchor proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C6 present established background knowledge about the actin cortex and its role in cell division. These are well-supported by the broader literature and provide appropriate context for the study. They are not novel findings of this work but rather motivate the experimental approach.

results.result: At low ATP concentrations, myofilaments function as active temporary crosslinkers that may drive actin self-assembly into clusters. Single muscle myosin II motors are traditionally non-processive, but assembling them into filaments makes them processive through coupling of multiple myosin heads. Actin structure formation after ATP depletion has been reported in solution-based experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C52-C53, and C76 cite established knowledge and prior work. C13 references predictions from Smith et al. 2007. C52-C53 describe well-established myosin motor properties. C76 provides relevant context from prior studies. These claims appropriately position the current work within existing literature.

results.result: Actin filaments have a persistence length of 15 µm (corresponding to bending rigidity EI=60 nN·µm²) and break when the radius of curvature decreases below 0.18 µm (curvature 5.6 µm⁻¹).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 cite well-established physical properties of actin filaments from literature (Yanagida et al. 1984; Arai et al. 1999). These values are standard in the field and appropriately used as model parameters. The relationship between persistence length and bending rigidity is correctly stated.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that synthetic myofilaments fragment and compact membrane-bound actin filaments at low ATP concentrations (0.1-1 µM), with breakage events observed in all experiments (n=21) and fluorescence intensity measurements showing compaction of fragments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the interesting mechanism but express major concern about lack of quantification (concern #1: 'There is concern at the lack of quantification of the major experiment. There is a need to quantify these results. How many times were these experiments performed and how many times were the effects of myofilaments on actin filaments observed?'). While the authors report n=21 experiments, reviewers indicate insufficient quantitative analysis of the core findings.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanism where tension builds up between myofilament ends, generating ~23 pN of compressive force sufficient to buckle and break actin filaments, with computational modeling supporting that single myofilaments can generate this force without requiring attachment to rigid structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers question the utility and validity of the simulations (concern #2: 'It is not clear how much the simulations have helped the paper. It would be more useful if the simulations lead to some testable hypothesis'). Additionally, concern #3 notes that 'the force estimate (23 pN) for buckling only reflects that of 5–6 active heads' with '>80% of the myosin heads are in rigor,' raising questions about the physiological relevance of the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Actin pattern formation occurred at ATP concentrations between 0.1-1 µM in 94% of experiments (n=45), with fragmentation and directed movement only observed at these low ATP concentrations, while being absent at higher and lower concentrations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly criticize the use of low ATP concentrations as non-physiological (concern #3: 'Given that the km for myosin-II nucleotide-binding is in the tens of micro-molar, the use of ∼3 micro-molar ATP is a concern. With respect to muscle...the ATP concentration is ∼5 mM and >100 micro-molar in non-muscle cells'). Concern #6 explicitly states 'the conditions used in the experiments were not very physiological and hard to reconcile with what is probably found in cells.'

results.result: The authors show that lowering ATP concentration increases myofilament processivity and duty ratio, with low ATP trajectories being longer and dwell times >900 ms being six times more frequent at low ATP (n=681) versus high ATP (n=102) conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers criticize this approach as creating 'near rigor conditions' (concern #3) that do not reflect physiological behavior. Concern #4 states 'The authors use myosin-II mini-filaments that are free in solution, which forces them to use rigor conditions,' and concern #5 questions 'The choice of muscle myosin-II seems specialized; perhaps non-muscle myosin-II would be best for reconstituting general cellular behavior.'

results.result: The authors developed a minimal actin cortex (MAC) system with actin filaments coupled to supported lipid bilayers via biotin-neutravidin bonds, with controllable actin density, and observed dynamic rearrangement and actomyosin foci formation upon addition of 500-600 nm myofilaments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers question the experimental design, with concern #4 stating 'shouldn't myosin-II be tethered independently of actin in their assays (as it is presumably to some degree at the cell division site, given that myosin localization is often tail-dependent and actin-independent)?' Concern #5 asks 'How closely does the actin and myosin concentration used reflect the in vivo actomyosin density at the cell cortex?' indicating uncertainty about the system's physiological relevance.

results.result: Computational simulations show that at low ATP concentrations, generated force continuously bends actin above the breakage threshold, while at intermediate concentrations force fluctuates near threshold, and at high concentrations insufficient curvature develops, with force increasing with decreasing ATP and velocity increasing linearly with ATP concentration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express skepticism about the simulations' contribution (concern #2: 'It is not clear how much the simulations have helped the paper. It would be more useful if the simulations lead to some testable hypothesis that then expand/strengthen/fine-tune the model'). The modeling results are questioned for their ability to provide meaningful insights beyond describing the experimental observations.

results.result: The authors propose that the observed fragmentation and compaction mechanism may contribute to actin turnover and cortex reorganization during cytokinesis and in other in vitro actomyosin systems, drawing parallels to myosin II-dependent actin bundle breakage in neuronal growth cones.
results.evaluation: Reviewers fundamentally question the physiological relevance of the findings. Concern #6 states 'We generally felt that the conditions used in the experiments were not very physiological and hard to reconcile with what is probably found in cells' and requests experiments with 'non-muscle myosin II at physiological ATP concentrations' to validate the biological relevance of these proposed mechanisms.

results.result: The modeling uses established biophysical parameters including actin bending rigidity (60 nN·µm²), myosin step size (5 nm), head stiffness (1 pN/nm), myofilament dimensions (560 nm length, 160 nm bare zone, ~30 interacting heads), and actin persistence length (15 µm) with breakage at curvature radius <0.18 µm.
results.evaluation: These are standard biophysical parameters from established literature that reviewers do not challenge. The parameters themselves are accepted, though reviewers question how they are applied in the non-physiological experimental conditions (concerns #3-6).

results.result: The manuscript presents established background knowledge about cell cortex structure, myosin motor function, and how myosin assembly into filaments creates processivity through coupling of multiple motor heads.
results.evaluation: These are background claims based on established knowledge and cited literature that reviewers do not dispute. They provide context for the experimental work but are not novel findings being evaluated.

results.result: The authors discuss that ATP levels vary in cells and that physiological ATP concentrations are typically millimolar, while suggesting that phosphorylation of myosin light chains may control processivity in cells to shift behavior to higher ATP concentrations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers directly challenge the relevance of these arguments. Concern #3 emphasizes that 'the ATP concentration is ∼5 mM and >100 micro-molar in non-muscle cells,' contradicting the authors' use of sub-micromolar concentrations. The speculation about phosphorylation (C42) does not address reviewers' fundamental concerns about experimental conditions.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect claim overlap (C38, C39, C42) regarding ATP concentrations and phosphorylation speculation. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN acknowledging lack of experimental validation. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, directly challenging the relevance given that cellular ATP is millimolar, not micromolar as used in experiments.

Perfect claim overlap (C5, C49, C50, C51) regarding biological relevance and generalizability. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging speculation lacks cellular validation. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, fundamentally questioning physiological relevance and requesting experiments with non-muscle myosin II at physiological ATP concentrations.

High overlap on experimental system design claims (C7-C9, C77-C79). OpenEval finds the MAC system well-characterized and SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, questioning whether myosin-II should be tethered independently and whether actin/myosin concentrations reflect in vivo cortex density.

High overlap on model parameters (C60-C71). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding parameters well-established from literature. Peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED for the parameters themselves, though they question how these are applied in non-physiological experimental conditions.

Overlap on ATP concentration dependence claims (C10-C12, C75). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED with systematic observations and adequate sample size. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, strongly criticizing low ATP concentrations as non-physiological compared to millimolar cellular levels.

Overlap on processivity and low ATP claims (C40, C41, C55, C59). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on established literature and experimental observations. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, criticizing the approach as creating 'near rigor conditions' that don't reflect physiological behavior.

Overlap on mechanistic model claims (C22-C30). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding the model internally consistent though some aspects inferential. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning whether simulations help the paper and noting that force estimates reflect only 5-6 active heads with >80% in rigor.

Overlap on fragment compaction and foci formation (C14-C16). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with direct experimental observations across n=21 experiments. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, expressing major concern about lack of quantification despite acknowledging the interesting mechanism.

Overlap on computational simulation claims (C34-C36, C72). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding simulations use well-established parameters and systematically explore parameter space. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning whether simulations lead to testable hypotheses that strengthen the model.

Overlap on single-molecule tracking and processivity (C17-C21). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with strong quantitative evidence. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, concerned about lack of quantification despite n=21 experiments being reported.

Overlap on background claims about actin cortex (C1, C6). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, recognizing these as established background knowledge from literature that appropriately contextualizes the study.

Overlap on simulation velocity results (C73, C74). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding linear velocity-ATP relationship consistent with standard myosin kinetics. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning the simulations' overall contribution to the paper.

Overlap on main findings and mechanism (C3, C4). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, viewing these as core contributions backed by experiments and modeling. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning simulation utility and noting force estimates reflect only a small fraction of active heads.

Overlap on established myosin properties (C52, C53). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, recognizing these as well-established knowledge from prior work that appropriately positions the current study.

Overlap on modeling conclusions (C43-C46). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding simulations successfully demonstrate force generation. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning whether simulations lead to testable hypotheses and noting concerns about the small number of active heads.
Overlap on actin physical properties (C70, C71). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these as well-established literature values appropriately used as model parameters.

Minimal overlap on main finding C2 (ATP-dependent fragmentation). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED as core contribution. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN due to lack of quantification, though they acknowledge the mechanism is interesting.

Overlap on trajectory and dwell time claims (C56-C58). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with strong single-molecule tracking data. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, criticizing the use of free myosin-II in solution forcing rigor conditions.

Minimal overlap on claim C10 (experimental design). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with systematic observations. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning whether the system reflects in vivo actomyosin density at cell cortex.

Minimal overlap on claim C31 (simulation parameters). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED using well-established physical parameters. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED for the parameters themselves, though context of concerns about non-physiological conditions remains.
